leadership-psych-safety.essentialQuestion: After a team lead starts thanking people for reporting near misses, reports rise from 2 to 9 a quarter. Is the team getting less safe, and what does research on psychological safety say this change is a sign of?

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an invented team that, judging from its logs, has about 12 near misses a quarter. Before the change, 2 were reported; after the lead began thanking people and asking what could be learned, 9 were. The counts are illustrative.
Derivation: the reporting rate rose from 2 / 12 ≈ 16.7% to 9 / 12 = 75%. The number of near misses stayed about the same; what changed is how many the team can learn from.
Independent check: compare the reports with the logs. If the logged near misses did not rise while reports did, the increase reflects willingness to speak up, not a deterioration in safety.

Misconception to reject: 'psychological safety means lowering standards' or 'being nice.' Edmondson defines team psychological safety as a shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking, such as admitting a mistake or asking a question, which supports high standards by making problems visible.

Change one factor: if a reporter is criticized in public after the change, and reports then fall to 3 a quarter, the rate drops to 25% while the near misses continue unseen. One reaction can undo the climate that produced the reports.

Source and limits: A. Edmondson, 'Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams', Administrative Science Quarterly 44(2), 1999, studied 51 work teams in a manufacturing company and found team psychological safety associated with learning behavior, which mediated its relationship with team performance: https://doi.org/10.2307/2666999. It is a field study in one company and shows association; the counts here are invented.

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: the validity figure comes from a meta-analysis summarized below; the comparison value of .20 is a hypothetical predictor used only to show the arithmetic.

Derivation: a validity of r = .42 is the correlation between interview scores and later job performance. Squaring it gives r² ≈ 0.176, so about 17.6% of the variation in performance is associated with the interview score. A hypothetical predictor with r = .20 would account for 4%.
Independent check: .42 × .42 = .1764, which matches. A correlation of .42 does not mean 42% of hires succeed; it means candidates who score higher tend, on average, to perform better.

Misconception to reject: 'a good interviewer can tell in the first few minutes.' Structure is what makes interviews comparable: the same job-related questions for every candidate, rating scales with defined anchors, and independent scoring by more than one interviewer before discussion.

Change one factor: the same summary notes a relatively high spread around the .42 average. An implementation at r = .25 would account for only about 6.25% of performance variation, which is why the quality of the structure matters.

Source and limits: an article in SIOP's The Industrial-Organizational Psychologist reports that Sackett, Zhang, Berry and Lievens (2022, Journal of Applied Psychology 107, 2040–2068) found structured interviews had the highest mean operational validity, r = .42, with a relatively high spread around that mean: https://www.siop.org/tip-article/is-cognitive-ability-the-best-predictor-of-job-performance. Validity in any one organization depends on how the interview is built and run.
